cell-communication-s1.title: Light from bacteria at increasing cell density
cell-communication-s1.text: The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri makes light with an enzyme called luciferase. Researchers grew three strains in flasks of seawater medium at 25 °C and measured cell density and light output as each culture grew. Strain W is the wild type. Strain N lacks the enzyme that makes the bacterium's autoinducer. Strain N+A is strain N grown with 5 µM synthetic autoinducer added to the medium at the start. Light per cell is given relative to strain W at the lowest density (set to 1). Points are means of 3 flasks.

cell-communication-s2.title: How far does an injected dye spread?
cell-communication-s2.text: Researchers grew a single flat layer of liver cells in a dish. They injected one cell with a fluorescent dye and, 5 minutes later, counted how many neighboring cells had become fluorescent. They tested four dyes of different sizes, in untreated cells and in cells given a drug that closes gap junctions 10 minutes before the injection. Each value is the mean for 10 injected cells.

table.caption: Number of neighboring cells fluorescent 5 minutes after one cell was injected

cell-communication-s3.title: Does a T cell need to touch?
cell-communication-s3.text: Helper T cells are white blood cells that become active when their receptor binds an antigen, a fragment of a pathogen's protein, displayed on the surface of an antigen-presenting cell. Researchers set up culture wells containing helper T cells that recognize one antigen. In some wells antigen-presenting cells were mixed in with the T cells. In others the two cell types were separated by a filter with pores 0.4 µm wide, which lets dissolved molecules through but not cells. After 24 hours they measured the percentage of T cells that had become active.

table.caption: Helper T cells active after 24 hours

items.q: Which statement best describes how light per cell in strain W changes as cell density increases?
options: It stays near 1 up to 3 × 10⁸ cells/mL, rises steeply from about 4 to 7 × 10⁸, then levels off.
It rises in proportion to density, so each doubling of density roughly doubles the light made by each cell.
It rises steeply at the lowest densities and then falls as the culture becomes more crowded.
It stays close to 1 at each density, because the light made by a cell depends on its own luciferase.

why.correct: Strain W reads 1-8 units up to 3 × 10⁸ cells/mL, climbs to 580 by 7 × 10⁸, and changes little after that (630, 650): low, then a steep switch, then a plateau.
options: This matches the points: a flat start, a steep rise from about 4 to 7 × 10⁸ cells/mL, and a plateau near 650.
From 3 to 6 × 10⁸ cells/mL density doubles but light per cell rises about 54-fold, far more than proportional.
The lowest densities give the lowest light per cell, and the curve never falls.
That describes strain N. Strain W's light per cell rises several hundred-fold.

items.q: By what factor does light per cell in strain W increase between 3 × 10⁸ and 6 × 10⁸ cells/mL? Give a whole number.

why.correct: Light per cell at 6 × 10⁸ ÷ light per cell at 3 × 10⁸ = 430 ÷ 8 = 53.75, about 54 times, while density only doubled.

items.q: Which comparison gives the strongest evidence that strain N can still detect the autoinducer and make light?
options: Strain N+A with strain N at the same low density
Strain N with strain W at 10 × 10⁸ cells/mL
Strain W at 1 × 10⁸ with strain W at 8 × 10⁸ cells/mL
Strain N at 1 × 10⁸ with strain N at 8 × 10⁸ cells/mL

why.correct: Adding autoinducer is the only difference between N and N+A. N+A glows brightly (about 560 units) at 1 × 10⁸ cells/mL where N makes 1, so N's receptor and light-making enzymes work; what N lacks is the signal itself.
options: The two differ only in added autoinducer, and N+A glows strongly, so detection and light-making must be intact.
This shows strain N is dark when dense, but not why: a broken receptor or broken luciferase would also make it dark.
This shows the density switch in the normal strain; it says nothing about what strain N can do.
Strain N stays dark at both densities, which fits a missing signal, a missing receptor or missing luciferase equally well.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for strain W's dim light at low density and bright light at high density?
options: Each cell releases autoinducer slowly; only when many cells share the volume does its concentration bind enough receptors to switch the light genes on.
Crowded cells run short of nutrients, and starving cells make light as a stress response that well-fed cells at low density do not show.
Light from neighboring cells is absorbed and released again by each cell, so each cell appears brighter when many cells surround it.
Cells that have divided many times have built up luciferase over each division, so older, denser cultures glow more per cell.

why.correct: Strain N, which cannot make autoinducer, stays dark when dense, and strain N+A glows when sparse. The signal's concentration, which rises with density, is what switches the light on.
options: This fits all three strains: no autoinducer means no light, added autoinducer means light at any density.
Strain N is just as crowded as strain W yet stays dark, and N+A glows at low density with plenty of nutrients, so starvation is not the trigger.
Strain N is dense with neighbors yet makes almost no light per cell, so neighbors' light is not what raises it.
Strain N goes through the same divisions and stays dark, so division alone does not build up light.

items.q: A fourth strain, R, makes autoinducer normally but lacks the receptor protein for it. Predict the light per cell of strain R grown with 5 µM added autoinducer.
options: Close to 1 at each density, because the autoinducer has nothing to bind in strain R
About 600 at each density, like strain N+A, because the autoinducer is present from the start
Close to 1 at low density, rising to about 650 at high density, like strain W
Higher than strain W at each density, because strain R gets autoinducer from two sources

why.correct: A signal acts only through its receptor. With no receptor, no amount of autoinducer can switch the light genes on, so strain R stays dark like strain N.
options: Without a receptor the signal cannot be detected, however much is present.
Strain N+A glows because its receptor works; strain R has no receptor to bind the added autoinducer.
Strain W's rise needs a working receptor; strain R makes signal it cannot detect.
Extra signal does nothing for a cell that cannot bind it.

items.q: Which statement best describes the results in untreated cells?
options: Dyes P and Q (457 daltons or less) reached over 20 neighbors; dyes R and S reached none.
Each dye reached about the same number of neighbors, whatever its size.
The larger the dye, the more neighboring cells it reached in 5 minutes.
Dye P reached fewer neighbors than dye S, because small dyes leak out of cells before they can spread.

why.correct: Untreated cells: dye P reached 24 neighbors and dye Q 22, while dyes R and S reached 0. There is a sharp cut-off between 457 and 3,000 daltons.
options: These are the untreated values: about 22-24 cells for the two small dyes and zero for the two large ones.
The counts range from 0 to 24, so size clearly matters.
The trend runs the other way: the two largest dyes reached no neighbors.
Dye P reached 24 cells and dye S reached none.

items.q: Calculate the percent decrease in the number of neighbors reached by dye P when the gap-junction blocker is added. Give a whole number.

why.correct: Percent decrease = (untreated − blocked) ÷ untreated × 100 = (24 − 1) ÷ 24 × 100 = 95.8%, about 96%.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the data?
options: Molecules below a size limit between about 460 and 3,000 daltons pass from cell to cell through gap junctions within minutes.
Gap junctions pump small dyes into neighboring cells using ATP, and the blocker works by stopping ATP production.
The dyes leak out of the injected cell and are taken up from the medium by its neighbors.
Large dyes do reach the neighbors through gap junctions, but more slowly than small dyes do.

why.correct: Small dyes spread to about 22-24 neighbors and the blocker cuts that to 1, so they travel through gap junctions; dyes of 3,000 daltons or more do not spread at all.
options: Both parts are supported: spread depends on open gap junctions, and only the small dyes spread.
Gap junctions are channels: molecules diffuse through them. Nothing in the data points to ATP or pumping.
Leaking and uptake from the medium would not be stopped by closing gap junctions, yet the blocker stopped nearly all spread.
The large dyes reached zero cells in 5 minutes; the data give no sign that they pass at all.

items.q: What is the main reason for including the cells given the gap-junction blocker?
options: To test whether the dye spreads through gap junctions rather than by some other route
To make sure the injected cell was still alive and healthy after the injection was made
To keep the size of the dye the same from one trial to the next
To measure how quickly each dye diffuses through the cytoplasm

why.correct: If closing gap junctions stops the spread, the dye must travel through them. Without this comparison, leaking out and re-entering would be just as possible.
options: The blocker condition isolates one route: if spread stops when gap junctions close, they were the route.
The blocker says nothing about whether the cell survived; a living cell with closed junctions also stops spread.
Dye size is the variable the researchers changed on purpose, set by which dye they chose, not by the blocker.
The experiment counts neighbors reached, not the speed of movement inside one cell.

items.q: Heart muscle cells are joined by gap junctions that let ions flow between them. Predict the effect of the same blocker on a sheet of beating heart muscle cells.
options: Their contractions would fall out of step, because the electrical change could not pass from cell to cell.
Each cell would contract faster, because ions could no longer escape into neighboring cells.
The cells would stop making ATP, because glucose could no longer enter them.
There would be no change in the beat, because hormones carried in the blood set the timing of each contraction.

why.correct: Ions are small, like dyes P and Q, so they pass through gap junctions. The ion flow carries the electrical change from one heart cell to the next; blocking it leaves cells contracting out of step.
options: Ions are small enough to pass, so closing the junctions breaks the cell-to-cell spread of the electrical signal.
Ion flow to neighbors is what spreads the beat; blocking it does not make any one cell contract faster.
Glucose enters heart cells through membrane transporters from the tissue fluid, not through gap junctions.
Hormones can change the heart rate, but each beat spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions within a fraction of a second.

items.q: Which conclusion is best supported by wells 3 and 4?
options: Activation needs contact with the presenting cells; molecules they release into the medium are not enough.
The filter killed most of the T cells, so they could not become active.
Antigen-presenting cells release a dissolved signal into the medium that activates T cells across the filter.
The antigen alone activates T cells, and the antigen-presenting cells play no part.

why.correct: Same cells and same antigen: 68% active when mixed, 5% across a filter that passes dissolved molecules. Only touching made the difference.
options: The two wells differ only in whether the cells can touch, and activation drops from 68% to 5%.
Nothing in the data shows the filter harmed the T cells; the simpler reading is that it kept them from touching the presenting cells.
Dissolved molecules cross the filter, yet only 5% of T cells became active, about the background level.
Well 1 has antigen without presenting cells and only 2% are active, so the antigen alone does not do it.

items.q: What possibility does well 2 rule out?
options: That touching an antigen-presenting cell activates T cells even when no antigen is displayed
That T cells become active on their own during 24 hours in culture
That the antigen is toxic to T cells at the concentration used
That the filter holds back dissolved molecules from the medium as well as the cells themselves

why.correct: In well 2 the cells touch but there is no antigen, and only 4% become active. So contact alone does not activate them: they need contact with a cell displaying the antigen they recognize.
options: Contact without antigen gives 4%, close to background, so the displayed antigen is required.
Well 1, T cells with antigen but no presenting cells, shows the background level; well 2 tests something else.
Well 3 has antigen and 68% active, so the antigen does not harm them; well 2 has no antigen at all.
There is no filter in well 2.

items.q: In a fifth well, cells are mixed and antigen is added, but the antigen-presenting cells were first given a drug that stops them displaying antigen fragments on their surface. They still take in the antigen. Predict the percentage of active T cells.
options: Low, close to well 2, because the T cells touch presenting cells but find no antigen displayed
High, close to well 3, because the antigen is still inside the presenting cells
High, close to well 3, because the presenting cells can still release signals into the medium
Intermediate, between wells 3 and 4, because half of the signal is still delivered

why.correct: The T cell's receptor must bind antigen on the presenting cell's surface. Antigen hidden inside the cell cannot be touched, so the result should look like contact without antigen (well 2).
options: Contact with a cell displaying no antigen is the situation in well 2, about 4% active.
The T cell cannot reach antigen inside another cell; it reads only what is displayed on the surface.
Well 4 already showed that released molecules activate few T cells.
Display is all or nothing here: without displayed antigen there is no match for the T cell receptor.

items.q: The body has helper T cells with millions of different receptors, each fitting a different antigen. How does requiring contact with a presenting cell make the immune response specific to the pathogen that is actually present?
options: Only T cells whose receptor fits the displayed antigen bind and become active, so the response is built from cells that recognize this pathogen.
Contact lets the presenting cell hand its own receptors to each T cell it touches, giving them the right shape.
Contact lets the antigen-presenting cell destroy T cells whose receptors do not fit the antigen.
A released signal would travel too slowly through the blood to reach T cells in time, so contact is faster.

why.correct: Activation needs a physical match between the T cell's receptor and the antigen on the surface it touches, so only matching T cells are switched on.
options: The match between receptor and displayed antigen selects which T cells respond.
Receptors are made by each T cell from its own genes; they are not handed over by contact.
Non-matching T cells are simply not activated; the data give no sign of their being destroyed.
Speed is not the issue: a released signal, as in well 4, would reach T cells whatever their receptor, which would make the response unspecific.

items.q: Which is an example of endocrine signaling?
options: The pancreas releases insulin into the blood, and it acts on muscle cells in the legs.
A neuron releases a neurotransmitter that binds receptors on the muscle cell next to it.
Two neighboring plant cells exchange sugar through plasmodesmata in their cell walls.
Platelets at a cut release a growth factor that makes nearby skin cells divide.

why.correct: Endocrine signaling is long-distance: a hormone travels in the blood to target cells far from where it was released.
options: Insulin travels in the blood from the pancreas to distant target cells: long-distance, endocrine signaling.
This is synaptic signaling: a neurotransmitter crossing a synaptic cleft to one target cell.
This is direct contact through channels joining the cytoplasms.
This is local signaling: a growth factor acting on nearby cells.

items.q: In a strain of mice, the muscle cells lack one protein. After a meal these mice release insulin normally and it reaches their muscle cells, yet the muscle cells do not respond to it. Which missing protein best explains this?
options: The receptor protein on the muscle cell surface that insulin binds
An enzyme in the blood that breaks insulin down after a meal
A channel that lets insulin pass into the muscle cell's nucleus
The protein in the pancreas that releases insulin by exocytosis

why.correct: Exposure is normal: insulin is released and reaches the muscle cells. A cell responds to a hormone only if it makes the matching receptor, so a missing receptor explains why these muscle cells ignore the insulin around them.
options: Without the receptor, insulin reaches the muscle cells but has nothing to bind, so they cannot respond.
Missing this enzyme would leave more insulin in the blood, not stop the muscle cells from responding to it.
Insulin is a protein that does not need to enter the nucleus; it acts by binding a receptor on the cell surface.
The pancreas is working: the mice release insulin normally after a meal, and the missing protein is in the muscle cells.

items.q: At a wound, platelets release a growth factor that is normally broken down by enzymes in the tissue fluid within minutes. Predict the effect of a drug that slows this breakdown.
options: Cells farther from the wound would bind the growth factor and start to divide.
Cells near the wound would stop dividing, because the growth factor would stay outside them.
The growth factor would enter the blood and act as a hormone on target cells in organs throughout the body.
No change, because the platelets themselves are the cells with receptors for the growth factor.

why.correct: A local signal stays local because it is diluted and destroyed as it spreads. Slower breakdown lets it reach a high enough concentration farther away, so more distant cells respond.
options: Lasting longer, the signal spreads farther before it falls too low to bind receptors.
The growth factor acts from outside by binding receptors; staying outside longer means more binding, not less.
Spreading somewhat farther through tissue is not the same as being carried around the body in the blood.
The growth factor acts on nearby skin and connective tissue cells, which have the receptors.

items.q: Select the two features that make synaptic signaling faster and more precisely aimed than endocrine signaling.
options: The neurotransmitter crosses a gap of a few tens of nanometers instead of traveling through the blood.
The neurotransmitter is released right next to a single target cell.
Neurotransmitters are much larger molecules than hormones.
Neurotransmitters act without binding to receptors.
The neurotransmitter enters the blood, which carries it quickly to its target.

why.correct: Speed comes from the tiny distance; precision comes from releasing the signal onto one cell. A hormone must travel through the blood and reaches target cells everywhere.
options: Diffusing across a tiny gap takes about a millisecond.
Release at one synapse limits the signal to one target cell.
Size is not what sets the speed; many neurotransmitters are small molecules.
Neurotransmitters work by binding receptors on the target cell, just as hormones do.
Traveling in the blood is endocrine signaling, the slower and broader route.

items.q: A small fluorescent sugar injected into one leaf cell appears in the neighboring cells within minutes, even though every plant cell is surrounded by a cell wall. Which structure best explains this?
options: Plasmodesmata, channels through the cell walls that join the cytoplasms of neighboring cells
Aquaporins, membrane channels that let water and dissolved sugars cross into the cell wall
Vesicles that release the sugar into the cell wall by exocytosis, followed by uptake into the next cell
A hormone that carries the sugar through the plant to cells with receptors

why.correct: Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasms of plant cells through their walls, the plant counterpart of gap junctions, so small molecules pass straight from cell to cell.
options: Plasmodesmata provide a direct cytoplasm-to-cytoplasm path through the wall.
Aquaporins pass water, not sugars, and they open into the wall rather than into the neighbor.
Exocytosis of a small dye followed by uptake would be slow and would scatter it into the wall, not deliver it straight to neighbors.
A hormone is a signal that binds receptors; it does not carry other molecules from cell to cell.

items.q: Put the events of synaptic signaling from a neuron to a muscle cell in order.
options: An electrical signal reaches the end of the neuron.
Vesicles fuse with the neuron's membrane and release neurotransmitter by exocytosis.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft.
The neurotransmitter binds receptor proteins on the muscle cell.
The muscle cell's behavior changes and it contracts.

why.correct: The electrical signal triggers release; the neurotransmitter must cross the cleft before it can bind; binding the receptor is what changes the target cell.
